title: Capacity injection and rotation playbook + incident review (draft)
content:
Scope and intent:
This is a practical, trimmed playbook for fast recovery from infra events that impact inference capacity: GPU faults and swaps, node cordon/drain during replacement, emergency cluster recovery when autoscaling/placement fails, and expedited capacity injection. It doubles as an incident notes template for on-call to capture timeline, decisions, and follow-ups.

When to use this doc:
- Node-level GPU hardware failures (OOM, ECC errors, HW scorch)
- Planned or emergency GPU replacement requiring physical swap and node reboot
- Node cordon & drain to evacuate workloads safely
- Cluster-level degraded capacity due to scheduling or placement regressions
- Rapid capacity-add exercises (burst pools or hot path scaling)

Quick decision tree (on-call):
1) Is traffic degraded or erroring? (latency spikes / 5xxs) => Pager escalation.
2) Does metrics show sustained token throttling or queue growth? => Consider capacity injection.
3) Is the issue isolated to one node/gpu or cross-cluster? => single-node flow vs cluster recovery.

Preflight checks (5m):
- Check control plane: console.health, api-gateway errors, redis/kv health, database.
- Metrics: per-model token/sec, queue length, e2e latency percentiles, retry rates.
- Node inventory: `kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep -i gpu` and `kubectl describe node <node>` for allocatable/gpu annotations.
- Pod placement: `kubectl get pods -o wide -n inference | grep <node>`

Single-node GPU failure: fast path (target MTTR under 35m)
A. Immediate mitigation (first 10m):
  - Cordon the node to stop new scheduling: `kubectl cordon <node>` (note operator: confirm this is not part of a larger scale operation).
  - Drain non-critical pods first (or use `--pod-selector` for inference pods): `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force` (oncall note: manual + watch for stuck terminating pods).
  - If GPU-attached pods use local caches, notify owning team (label: service-owner).
  - If possible, trigger fallback routing to dedicated warm pool or lower-capacity model variant via routing override in Console (short-term).

B. Diagnostics (parallel with A):
  - Check driver/kernel logs: `dmesg | tail -n 200`, `journalctl -u nvidia-persistenced` (if using NVIDIA) or vendor logs for other accelerators.
  - Run GPU health probe: `nvidia-smi -q --gpu=0` or accelerator-specific diag. Capture error codes.
  - If device shows ECC or thermal fault, mark hardware for replacement.
  - If errors indicate transient (firmware watchdog) attempt soft reset: `sudo nvidia-smi --gpu-reset -i 0` (only if supported; document oncall must confirm safe).

C. Replace/Rotate GPU (if hardware fault confirmed) — coordination with hardware ops (30–120m):
  - Open ticket with datacenter ops and include node serial, rack, and timestamp.
  - Schedule short maintenance window if replacement requires power cycle.
  - If hot-swap capable: follow vendor hot-swap guide. If not: plan for full power cycle and node reimage if needed.
  - After physical swap, verify BIOS/firmware versions and re-flash if vendor recommends.
  - After bring-up: validate with `nvidia-smi`, driver load, smoke tests (small inference load), and model KV cache warming.

D. Bring node back:
  - Uncordon when ready: `kubectl uncordon <node>` and monitor Pod reschedules.
  - Confirm schedulable GPU resources and that inference pods reach Ready.
  - Smoke test: run 5 short model inferences (~1s each) across 3 models and check latencies/outputs.

Cluster recovery (when placement/ASG/autoscaler misbehaves):
- Symptoms: many pending pods with `0/1` GPU allocatable, or autoscaler failing to launch nodes.
- Fast mitigations:
  1) Evaluate quotas: cloud account VM/GPU quotas often silent cause. Check cloud console for quota errors or failed instance launches.
  2) If quota is exhausted, request emergency quota bump (follow SLA with cloud provider) while throttling load to preserve critical capacity.
  3) If autoscaler misconfig, manually scale worker pool: `terraform apply -target=module.gpu_pool` or cloud UI scale to force-add nodes into pool.
  4) Re-run node bootstrap scripts on new nodes (user-data logs), verify Kubelet registers GPUs (check kubelet logs).

Rapid capacity injection flow (burst capacity during spikes):
- Use Canary warm pool: route a small portion of traffic to lower-cost or lower-latency warm nodes first.
- If warm pool insufficient: trigger on-call 'capacity-inject' script in ops repo which sequences cloud instance launches, bootstrap, and k8s join.
- Acceptance criteria for injecting N nodes: each node should appear Ready and show expected GPU allocatable count within 8 minutes of launching.

On-call checklist during injection:
- Watch token cost impact (billing alarms) and notify finance if projected > threshold.
- Ensure new nodes are labeled and tainted correctly (`gpu=true, inference=true`) to prevent unexpected scheduling.
- Run a small synthetic traffic ramp to validate performance and model correctness.

Post-incident capture (immediately after mitigation):
- Record timeline: detection, eskalation, mitigations invoked, owner for each action, and timestamps.
- Note decisions and why (e.g. swapped hardware vs driver reset).
- Collect artifact links: instance IDs, support ticket IDs, driver logs, kube events.
- Identify follow-ups: permanent replacement schedule, capacity policy changes, autoscaler tuning, postmortem doc owner.

Operational runbook snippets (copy/paste commands):
- List GPU nodes: `kubectl get nodes -l accelerator=gpu -o wide`
- Cordon: `kubectl cordon <node>`
- Drain: `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data`
- Uncordon: `kubectl uncordon <node>`
- Check pod placement: `kubectl get pods -n inference -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>`
- Check kubelet and docker/containerd logs: `journalctl -u kubelet -n 500` and `journalctl -u containerd -n 200`
- Check cloud instance health: cloud CLI `aws ec2 describe-instance-status --instance-ids i-xxxx` or GCP equivalent

Common gotchas & FAQ (from previous incidents):
- Stuck terminating DaemonSets during drain: use `kubectl delete pod <pod> --grace-period=0 --force` but coordinate with team owning the daemonset.
- GPU reset unsupported in some kernel-drivers; avoid unless docs confirm.
- Kube scheduler delay: sometimes pending pods stay pending due to stale device-plugin caches; restart device plugin DaemonSet on each node (`kubectl rollout restart ds/device-plugin -n kube-system`).
- Autoscaler races: avoid simultaneous manual and autoscaler changes; communicate in #sre-oncall channel.

Acceptance criteria for returning incident to Monitoring-only:
1) All affected service-level indicators (p99 latency, queued tokens, 5xx rate) are back to baseline for 30 minutes.
2) All replaced hardware shows no recurring errors for 24 hours.
3) Follow-up tasks created and assigned for permanent remediation.

Postmortem template (to copy into incident ticket)
- Short summary (2–3 lines)
- Detection timeline (timestamps)
- Root cause (hardware / driver / scaling / config)
- Immediate mitigations (who did what)
- Impact (customers, API keys, routes)
- Action items (owner, due date, priority)
- Learning and preventative measures

Action items I propose after this run (examples):
- Add automated GPU health probe to alert on ECC warnings earlier (owner: Jordan)
- Add warm-pool autoscale policy and test monthly (owner: Diego)
- Document vendor hot-swap instructions in private-deployments runbooks (owner: Asha)

On-call notes (freeform) - use these lines when filing ticket:
- "Observed sustained queue growth starting 2025-02-11T03:12Z; one node (rack12-node08) showed ECC errors and GPU reset failures. Cordoned at 03:25Z, drained at 03:29Z. Vendor swap completed 04:22Z, node back by 04:55Z. No customer-facing errors persisted after 04:40Z."
- "Root cause likely GPU firmware mismatch combined with a hot kernel update earlier in the week. Confirm firmware/driver matrix in next retro."

Appendix: helpful links and snippets
- Ops repo capacity-inject: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops-playbooks/tree/main/capacity-inject
- Device plugin troubleshooting: confluence:infra/device-plugin-troubleshooting
- Emergency contact: datacenter-onsite@example.com (phone escalation list in internal directory)

Version notes: v0.3-draft — intended for SRE review. Replace placeholders and tighten thresholds once we run one full capacity injection drill.
